cf.title: Add archive_mode to prevent unarchived WAL on permanent primary failure

input.subject: Streaming replication and WAL archive interactions

verdict_reasoning: The problem is stated and three fleet operators report it, so level 1 holds. At level 2, four design points are open in v8: the archive_command contract (prior-attempts-1), the 'a' message reaching clients that did not ask (standards-compat-1), unbounded WAL retention (maintenance-fit-3) and ancestor timeline marking (replication-ondisk-3). Shared mode was set aside in message #31 in favour of always mode, so the list also needs to agree on already-exists-1. All of these are fixable.

brief.title: Add archive_mode = shared so standbys keep WAL until the primary archives it
brief.problem: With streaming replication and one WAL archive for primary and standby, a promoted standby does not archive WAL it got by streaming. Segments the primary had not archived before it failed are missing from the archive, which breaks point-in-time recovery. Borodin reports gaps in the PITR timeline for 1–2% of clusters after large datacenter outages.
brief.proposed_design: A new archive_mode value, shared, makes the standby mark streamed segments .ready and mark them .done only when the upstream reports them archived, so they are not removed earlier. The walsender sends the last archived segment in a new replication message, and cascading standbys relay it. On promotion the standby archives what the primary did not, and v8 adds a fallback where a standby archives itself when no reports arrive.
user_visible_surface: archive_mode gains the value shared; Heikki's original patch also forbade on during recovery, and v8's handling of on is not stated.
New replication protocol message 'a' (WAL archival report) carrying the last archived segment, sent by the walsender.
New GUC archive_status_report_interval (default 10s) that sets report frequency; in v8 the standby also uses it to request reports.
Startup fails with FATAL when a standby requests reports and the upstream does not archive.
author_claims: Shared mode fixes PITR gaps after losing the primary, seen in 1–2% of clusters in large outages.
archive_mode = always with a deduplicating archive tool works, but would raise requests to the archive storage about 2.5 to 3 times.
Fixing this in external HA tools fails because the standby may already have removed the WAL.
v4 ran in production for about 3 to 4 months and was mostly fine, apart from the bugs fixed later.
Several operators of large fleets (Harinath Kanchu, Grigory Smolkin) report the same problem and external workarounds.
brief.thread_state: Heikki proposed shared mode in 2014 but committed only always and the .partial change in 2015; Borodin revived shared mode in 2026, and Reshke posted v6 to v8. Borodin's last review of v8 lists open items: fallback timing after idle periods, report scheduling, ancestor timeline marking, missing docs and Windows test paths.
unclear: Whether v8 makes the 'a' message opt-in for all clients, so pg_receivewal and third-party protocol clients no longer break.
No bound on WAL a shared-mode standby keeps when the archive is down; the thread offers no cap like max_slot_wal_keep_size.
Why marking an ancestor timeline's switchpoint segment as done is safe, given the ancestor filename may be absent from the archive.
How shared mode behaves when the standby falls back to reading WAL from the archive with restore_command.
The fallback archiving in v8 lets primary and cascading standby both archive, which needs an archive_command that accepts identical duplicate files.
No performance numbers for the walsender reports or the archive_status directory scans.

prior_attempts.title: Better fix for "unarchived WAL files get deleted on crash recovery" bug.
prior_attempts.quote: We create a .done file for files streamed or restored from archive, so the WAL file recycling logic used during normal operation works just as well during archive recovery.
prior_attempts.reason:
Revert my earlier fix for the bug that unarchived WAL files get deleted on
crash recovery, commit c9cc7e05c6d82a9781883a016c70d95aa4923122. We create
a .done file for files streamed or restored from archive, so the WAL file
recycling logic used during normal operation works just as well during
archive recovery.

Per Fujii Masao's suggestion.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P1 relies on creating .done for streamed segments so that recycling in recovery works as in normal operation. Shared mode creates .ready for them instead, and the v4 XLogArchiveCheckDone bug (messages #36, #38) came from that change.

objections.title: Shared mode still needs a duplicate-tolerant archive_command, the reason it was dropped
objections.failure_scenario: An operator follows the documented archive_command, which refuses to overwrite an existing file. The primary archives a segment and dies before its report reaches the standby, or a v8 fallback standby archives in parallel with the primary. After promotion the standby's archiver retries the same file indefinitely, .ready files pile up in pg_wal, and the operator learns of it when the disk fills.
objections.argument: In message #31, shared mode was set aside because always mode plus a race-free, duplicate-tolerant archive command does the job, and shared mode was kept only for its "less strict requirements for the archive_command". Messages #29 and #30 showed shared mode still needs that tolerance at promotion, and message #20 objected to adding more archive_command logic that users must get right. v8 widens the need, because its fallback (message #41) lets the primary and a cascading standby both archive. The author's stated gain over always mode is a 2.5-3x cut in archive requests (message #39), not a simpler archive_command.
objections.author_must_show: With the documented example archive_command, what happens after promotion or v8 fallback when the segment already exists in the archive, and does the patch ship a command that handles this?

critic.reasoning: Message #29 confirms the archiver gets stuck on a duplicate after promotion, and message #42 shows the v8 fallback can race the primary. The proposal names no archive_command contract for shared mode, and a new patch version or documentation can state one.

objections.title: Unsolicited 'a' replication message breaks existing physical protocol clients
objections.failure_scenario: An operator runs pg_receivewal, or a third-party backup tool, with a permanent slot against a primary that has archive_mode = shared. The walsender sends an 'a' message, and the client stops with "unrecognized streaming header". With the retry loop it reconnects and fails again without progress, so the WAL copy silently stalls.
objections.argument: Message #40 reproduced this with pg_receivewal and noted that the PG 18 'p'/'s' pair is sent only on request, to avoid this hazard. Message #41 adds a standby-side request parameter in v8 but does not say whether the walsender still sends 'a' to clients that did not ask. Fixing receivelog.c covers in-core tools only. Older pg_receivewal binaries and external clients keep failing.
objections.author_must_show: In v8, does the walsender send 'a' only to clients that asked for it in START_REPLICATION, and what does an old pg_receivewal see?

critic.reasoning: Message #40 reproduced the pg_receivewal failure. Message #41 adds a standby-side request, which suggests opt-in, but no message says the walsender stopped sending 'a' to clients that did not ask.

objections.title: No bound on WAL a shared-mode standby keeps
objections.failure_scenario: The archive storage goes down for a day. Every shared-mode standby keeps all streamed WAL and fills its disk. Because archive_mode is PGC_POSTMASTER, the operator cannot turn retention off without a restart, and HA fails over to the next standby, which repeats the cycle.
objections.argument: Message #40 (point 7) reports this from production and says downstream added a SIGHUP GUC to escape it. Message #41's v8 handles only an upstream that never reports. It does not cap retention when reports stop because archiving stalls. Replication slots needed max_slot_wal_keep_size for the same class of problem.
objections.author_must_show: What limits WAL growth on a shared-mode standby during a long archive outage, and how does an operator release it without a restart?

critic.reasoning: Message #40, point 7, reports this from production, and v8 in message #41 covers only an upstream that never reports. A cap or a reloadable setting in a new version can fix it.

objections.title: Marking ancestor switchpoint segment done may leave an archive gap
objections.failure_scenario: After a timeline switch, the standby marks the ancestor-timeline segment holding the switchpoint as .done because the upstream reported the descendant segment archived. If the ancestor filename was never archived, a later PITR with recovery_target_timeline set to the ancestor cannot find it.
objections.argument: Message #42 points out that a descendant report only proves the shared prefix exists under the descendant filename. No explanation or archive-only recovery test was given. This marks a segment as safe to recycle without proof, the gap the feature exists to prevent, and message #12 names PITR to the old timeline as a real use.
objections.author_must_show: What guarantees that the ancestor-timeline filename of the switchpoint segment is in the archive before the standby recycles it?

critic.reasoning: Message #42 raises this against v8 and the thread holds no answer or archive-only recovery test. An explanation or a test in a new version can settle it.

objections.title: archive_mode = always with an idempotent archive_command already covers this
objections.failure_scenario: An operator sets archive_mode = always on primary and standby, with a shared archive and an archive_command that returns success when an identical file already exists. After the primary is lost, the archive has no gap. The only cost is more archive requests, so core would carry a second mode, protocol message and GUC to save storage requests.
objections.argument: Message #31 says that always plus a race-free, duplicate-tolerant archive_command makes shared unnecessary. Message #32 and message #39 do not say always fails; they say it costs 2.5 to 3 times more requests to the archive storage. That is a cost of one tool's design, which a HEAD check would reduce, as message #32 notes. The v8 fallback in message #41 also lets primary and cascading standby archive the same segments, so a duplicate-tolerant archive_command is needed anyway.
objections.author_must_show: Given that v8 already needs a duplicate-tolerant archive_command, what can shared mode do that archive_mode = always with that command cannot do, beyond fewer archive requests?

critic.reasoning: Messages #32 and #39 state only a cost reason against always, so the question is fair. Its weight is lower because three fleet operators report the problem, and the extra requests come from always mode itself, not from one tool.

other_surviving.title: No committer who knows archiving and timelines is engaged
other_surviving.failure_scenario: After commit, a report arrives that PITR to an ancestor timeline fails because the switchpoint segment was marked done but never archived under that name. The committer who pushed it must work out timeline-switch semantics alone, and the reviewers in the thread are not committers.
other_surviving.argument: The 2026 thread has the authors and peer reviewers only. Heikki, who designed shared mode, dropped it in message #31, and no committer has replied since message #31. Message #42 still lists open design questions in archiver, walsender and timeline code: ancestor-timeline marking, report scheduling and fallback timing. Those are the parts that need an owner with deep knowledge.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Which committer familiar with archiving and timeline switches has reviewed the v8 design, and do they agree with ancestor-timeline marking?

critic.reasoning: The thread shows no committer reply after message #31, and message #42 leaves timeline and walsender questions open. Under the rubric this belongs in the committability field and must not raise the verdict.

other_surviving.title: Expose primary_last_archived and use wal_keep_size, without a new mode
other_surviving.failure_scenario: An HA tool reads primary_last_archived on the standby, and wal_keep_size keeps recent WAL there. At promotion the tool archives the segments after the last reported one. If archive lag exceeds wal_keep_size, a gap appears, but a shared mode with the cap asked for in message #40 has the same gap.
other_surviving.argument: Message #33 says that exposing last_archived_wal on the standby alone would unblock external solutions. The author's reply is that external tools fail because the standby already removed the WAL. wal_keep_size already keeps WAL on a standby, with a bound. Unbounded retention is the open operational problem in message #40, item 7.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Why are the report message, the view column and wal_keep_size not enough for HA tools, and which failures need the in-core shared mode?

critic.reasoning: Message #33 asks for this smaller step, and the thread does not say why it is not enough. The comparison is only partly fair, because wal_keep_size keeps a fixed amount and leaves a gap when archive lag exceeds it.

refuted.title: Fallback archiving makes shared mode depend on duplicate-tolerant archive_command
refuted.failure_scenario: A user sets up an on -> on -> shared cascade with the archive_command from the documentation, which refuses to overwrite. The v8 fallback lets the cascading standby archive segments the primary also archives. The command fails on the duplicate, the archiver retries forever, and .ready files pile up on the standby.
refuted.argument: The 2015 design (message #1 docs) said a shared-mode standby does not archive while in recovery. Message #41 changes that, so primary and standby can archive the same file. Message #42 shows that the fallback timer can fire after an idle period while the primary is still archiving. Message #20 objected to adding more behaviour that only works if users write their archive_command correctly. Message #31 dropped shared mode for this reason and kept always.
refuted.author_must_show: What archive_command contract does shared mode require in v8, and how does a user with the documented non-overwriting command find out before the archiver gets stuck?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of prior-attempts-1, which covers both the promotion case and the v8 fallback case.

refuted.title: Meaning of archive_mode = on during recovery is not stated
refuted.failure_scenario: A user restores a base backup taken from a primary with archive_mode = on, the most common setting, and starts it as a standby or for PITR. If v8 keeps the 2015 rule, startup fails with FATAL. If v8 changes what on does in recovery, existing standbys behave differently after upgrade.
refuted.argument: Heikki's patch forbade on in recovery (docs hunk, message #5), and message #10 pointed out that this breaks restores of existing base backups. Message #14 and message #15 asked that on keep its current behaviour. The v6 to v8 messages do not say which rule applies now.
refuted.author_must_show: In v8, does a standby with archive_mode = on start and behave exactly as in Postgres 19?

critic.reasoning: Message #41 describes an on -> on -> shared cascade as a setup v8 handles, so a standby with archive_mode = on starts in v8. No 2026 message proposes changing what on does in recovery, so the second branch has no support.

refuted.title: Shared mode still needs a duplicate-tolerant archive_command
refuted.failure_scenario: The primary archives a segment and dies before the report reaches the standby, or v8 fallback archiving runs on a cascading standby while the primary also archives. With the documented `test ! -f` style archive_command, the second copy fails. The archiver retries forever and WAL piles up on the new primary.
refuted.argument: Message #29 confirms the archiver gets stuck in this case. Message #31 dropped shared mode because duplicate-safe archiving made it unnecessary. v8 fallback (message #41) makes double archival a normal path, and message #42 shows it can race the primary after an idle period. Message #20 objects to leaving correctness to user scripts, and the proposal still ships no duplicate-safe archive_command.
refuted.author_must_show: Which archive_command is documented as correct for shared mode, and what does the archiver do when it meets an identical file already in the archive?

refuted.title: No bound on WAL a shared-mode standby retains
refuted.failure_scenario: The archive storage is down for hours while the primary keeps trying to archive. Every shared-mode standby keeps all .ready segments, and v8 fallback archiving fails against the same archive. Each standby fills its disk, and the operator finds out when replicas go down during the outage.
refuted.argument: Message #40 reports this from production: archive_mode is PGC_POSTMASTER, so there is no runtime way out, and the authors added a downstream SIGHUP escape hatch. v8-0003 covers an upstream that does not archive at all, but not an archive that fails. Nothing like max_slot_wal_keep_size is proposed, so the setting meant to protect PITR can take down replicas too.
refuted.author_must_show: What caps standby WAL retention when archiving fails, and how does the operator change that cap without a restart?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-3, which also describes the repeated failover.

refuted.title: Unsolicited 'a' replication message breaks existing protocol clients
refuted.failure_scenario: A site runs pg_receivewal or a third-party WAL receiver with a permanent slot against a shared-mode primary. The walsender pushes an 'a' message, the client drops the connection with "unrecognized streaming header", and it reconnects in a loop with no progress. The site finds out when its archive or backup stops advancing.
refuted.argument: Message #40 reproduced this against pg_receivewal. It notes that the 'p'/'s' exchange added in PG 18 is sent only on request, likely to avoid this problem. Message #41 adds a standby-side request parameter, but the material does not show that the walsender sends 'a' only to clients that asked for it. Changing receivelog.c does not fix clients outside the tree.
refuted.author_must_show: Does v8 send the 'a' message only to clients that requested it in START_REPLICATION, so unchanged physical-protocol clients never receive it?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1, which also covers older pg_receivewal binaries.

refuted.title: v8 fallback brings back dual archiving that shared mode was meant to avoid
refuted.failure_scenario: In an on->on->shared cascade, the v8 fallback lets the cascading standby archive the same segments as the primary. An operator with a plain `test ! -f && cp` archive_command sees the archiver fail on every duplicate. WAL then piles up on the standby, and the operator finds out when the disk fills.
refuted.argument: Message #31 kept shared mode alive because it 'has less strict requirements for the archive_command' than always. Message #41 now archives from both primary and cascading standby, so shared mode again needs an idempotent archive_command. Message #42 shows the idle-period race in the fallback timer. Once fallback can archive duplicates, the cost gap with always plus a deduplicating tool, which is the stated motivation in message #39, gets smaller.
refuted.author_must_show: With the fallback in place, which archive_command requirements does shared mode still drop compared with always, and how often does fallback archiving run in your fleet?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of prior-attempts-1. Its extra point about a smaller cost gap is not supported, because the fallback archives only when no reports arrive.

refuted.title: WAL recycling gains a third mode that future changes can miss
refuted.failure_scenario: A later patch changes XLogArchiveCheckDone or restartpoint recycling and tests only on and always. Shared-mode standbys then remove .ready segments before the primary archives them. Nobody notices until a PITR after failover finds a gap.
refuted.argument: This has already happened once. Message #36 found that an existing early return in XLogArchiveCheckDone let restartpoints delete unarchived WAL, and v4 ran in production for months with that bug (message #39). A second cascading bug went unnoticed until message #38. The failure is silent, because WAL is removed and the gap only shows up at restore time.
refuted.author_must_show: What check makes a future change to WAL recycling fail loudly in tests or at runtime when it breaks shared-mode retention?

critic.reasoning: Message #38 adds TAP test 056, which runs the restartpoint path where the XLogArchiveCheckDone bug removed .ready segments, and reworks the cascading tests. Message #41 registers the tests in meson.build, so a later change that breaks retention fails in CI.

touch_points.reason: see objection replication-ondisk-3: Marking ancestor switchpoint segment done may leave an archive gap

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: Changes when a standby marks streamed segments .ready and .done, and so when it removes WAL.

touch_points.label: wire protocol
touch_points.reason: Adds replication message 'a' (WAL archival report) sent by the walsender.

touch_points.label: catalog changes
touch_points.reason: Adds column primary_last_archived to the system view pg_stat_wal_receiver.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: Adds an archive_mode value in xlog.h, and external physical replication clients must handle the new message.

touch_points.label: new GUC
touch_points.reason: Adds archive_status_report_interval and a new value shared for archive_mode.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: see objection standards-compat-1: Unsolicited 'a' replication message breaks existing physical protocol clients

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: WAL recycling, walsender, walreceiver and timeline handling gain a third archive mode with a fallback path.

touch_points.reason: The walsender sends periodic reports and the standby scans archive_status; the thread shows no numbers.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: Message #31 says archive_mode = always with a duplicate-tolerant archive_command covers the same case.

questions: In v8, does the walsender send 'a' only to clients that asked for it in START_REPLICATION, and what does an old pg_receivewal see?
Which archive_command contract does shared mode need at promotion and in the v8 fallback, and does the documented non-overwriting example meet it?
What caps WAL retention on a shared-mode standby during a long archive outage, and can an operator change that cap without a restart?
What guarantees that the ancestor-timeline filename of the switchpoint segment is in the archive before the standby marks it .done?
Since v8 needs a duplicate-tolerant archive_command, what does shared mode give over archive_mode = always beyond fewer archive requests?

committability.owner_note: It needs a committer who knows the archiver, WAL recycling at restartpoints, timeline switches and the walsender protocol. No committer has replied since message #31.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a new replication message, a new GUC and a third WAL recycling mode on standbys. Errors there show up as PITR gaps at restore time or as full disks on standbys, possibly years later.
committability.author_follow_up: Good sign: two authors posted v6 to v8, fixed bugs found in production use of v4, and keep the CommitFest entry current.

priority.reason: Operators of large fleets report PITR gaps after failover, so the goal has users. The patch touches xlog.c, walsender and walreceiver, and message #42 lists open design items, so a committer who knows the area is unlikely to start before those are settled.

provisional_note: No code was read, and the documentation hunks shown are from the 2015 patch, so v8 behaviour is known only from thread messages. The opt-in rule for 'a', the fallback timing and the timeline marking could not be checked.

precedents_retrieved.title: Track number of WAL files ready to be archived in pg_stat_archiver
precedents_retrieved.summary: The proposal adds the size of the archive queue, meaning the number of WAL files with a .ready status file in pg_xlog/archive_status, to the pg_stat_archiver view. Fujii Masao suggested two ways to get the value: count the .ready files, or keep a counter that goes up when a .ready file is created and down when it becomes .done.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The idea came up after pg_stat_archiver was committed. Michael Paquier added it to the TODO list under "Statistics Collector", and Gabriele Bartolini said he would try it later. No patch or objection appears in the shown messages.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Reduce checkpoints and WAL traffic on low activity database server"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Reduce checkpoints and WAL traffic on low activity database server"
Reverted commit(s): Reduce checkpoints and WAL traffic on low activity database server Previously, we skipped a checkpoint if no WAL had been written since last checkpoint, though this does not appear in user documentation. As of now, we skip a checkpoint until we have written at least one enough WAL to switch the next WAL file. This greatly reduces the level of activity and number of WAL messages generated by a very low activity server. This is safe because the purpose of a checkpoint is to act as a starting place for a recovery, in case of crash. This patch maintains minimal WAL volume for replay in case of crash, thus maintaining very low crash recovery time.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 18fb9d8d21a28caddb72c7ffbdd7b96d52ff9724.  Per
discussion, it does not seem like a good idea to allow committed changes to
go un-checkpointed indefinitely, as could happen in a low-traffic server;
that makes us entirely reliant on the WAL stream with no redundancy that
might aid data recovery in case of disk failure.

This re-introduces the original problem of hot-standby setups generating a
small continuing stream of WAL traffic even when idle, but there are other
ways to address that without compromising crash recovery, so we'll revisit
that issue in a future release cycle.

precedents_retrieved.objection:
Revert ill-starred change of 13-Feb-02: it appeared to fix a problem of
incorrect permissions checking, but in fact disabled most all permissions
checks for view updates.  This corrects problems reported by Sergey
Yatskevich among others, at the cost of re-introducing the problem
previously reported by Tim Burgess.  However, since we'd lived with that
problem for quite awhile without knowing it, we can live with it awhile
longer until a proper fix can be made in 7.5.

roaster_notes.note: The thread holds its own prior attempt: Heikki's 2014-2015 shared mode, cut back to always mode in message #31 and revived in message #32. The objection above covers the reason it was set aside.
Objections listed; config.sgml and monitoring.sgml docs for the new GUC and column are still missing per message #42, so the full user-facing contract cannot be checked yet.

Within the security angle I found no new exposure. The 'a' message travels only on replication connections, which already need the REPLICATION attribute. primary_last_archived matches last_archived_wal, which pg_stat_archiver already shows, and archive_command stays under superuser control. Unbounded WAL retention on a standby is an availability problem caused by an archive outage or a wrong configuration, not by an unprivileged user, so it belongs to the design angle.
Four objections listed. The demand is real: several large fleets report it in messages #33, #37 and #39.
Two objections from the already-exists angle. Both rest on mechanisms the thread itself names, and neither is fatal.

The material shows real, independent demand. Borodin reports PITR gaps in 1–2% of clusters after large outages (message #32), and Kanchu (message #33) and Smolkin (message #37, tens of thousands of clusters) report the same gap and external workarounds. Heikki called the shared-archive setup very common in 2014 (message #1). The archive_mode = always workaround costs about 2.5 to 3 times the archive requests (message #39). Costs fall mostly on shared-mode users; protocol and retention risks belong to other angles.
